one_liner: 2014-2016 prototype of Mula's first/last-byte SWAR substring filter, claimed 2-3x over std::string::find; buggy, superseded by sse4-strstr.
what_it_does: A single function, size_t strstr64(const char* s, size_t n, const char* needle) (plus a 4-byte strstr32), returns the offset of the first occurrence of a NUL-terminated needle in a haystack of known length, or NOT_FOUND (~size_t(0), the same value as std::string::npos). It is an experiment in the toys snippets repository with a timing harness (test.cpp, analyze.py) and a checker (verify.cpp), not a packaged library.
how_it_is_fast: It is a filter-then-verify search in the Karp-Rabin style where the hash is replaced by a test on the needle's first and last bytes: it XORs 8 haystack bytes at offset i and 8 bytes at offset i+k-1 against broadcast copies of those two needle bytes, ORs the results, and uses the classic SWAR has-zero-byte trick ((v - 0x01..) & ~v & 0x80..) to find candidate positions eight at a time. Only flagged candidates go to memcmp, so on natural text most positions are rejected with plain 64-bit integer operations and no SIMD instructions. This is the generic first/last-byte idea that the author's later sse4-strstr project and the Rust memchr crate's packed-pair prefilter build on.
when_to_use: Reading or teaching the first/last-byte filter in its simplest scalar SWAR form (about 35 lines).
As a starting point only after porting the fixes from sse4-strstr's swar64-strstr-v2.cpp: exact zero-byte test, a loop bound that covers the last position, and k=0, k=1 and n<k handled.

Non-x86 targets with a weak libc strstr: the fixed successor beat std::string::find 1.70x on ARMv7 (GCC 4.9.2) and 3.93x on ARMv8 (clang 3.8.0) in the sse4-strstr result files (derived from page data).
when_not_to_use: Any production use of this copy: by emulating its arithmetic, it returns wrong offsets (false positives), misses matches at the last start position, and runs off the end of the buffer when the needle is longer than the haystack.

Modern x86-64 hosts: in the author's own later results the fixed SWAR successor was 2.12x slower than the std::strstr (libc) row on Skylake i7-6700, 3.04x slower on Haswell i7-4770, 3.0x on Westmere M540 and 2.53x on Cascade Lake Gold 5217 (derived from page data; libc version not stated); only the Bulldozer FX-8510 run with GCC 4.8.4 was faster (3.2x).
Haystacks without at least 5 readable bytes after the NUL terminator (memory-mapped files ending at a page boundary, exact-size buffers under ASan).
Empty needles, needles longer than the haystack, haystacks over 4 GiB (the loop counter is a 32-bit unsigned int), or strict-alignment CPUs (unaligned uint64_t loads through a type-punned pointer).
When a maintained search is available: sse4-strstr's SIMD and SWAR v2 versions, sliceslice, or the libc/STL routine.

integration.dependencies: none beyond <cstring> and <cstdint>; the file has no includes and expects the caller to define NOT_FOUND
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (uses auto); Makefile builds with g++ -std=c++11 -O3; analyze.py needs Python 2 (print statements)
integration.platforms: little-endian with cheap unaligned 64-bit loads (x86-64, AArch64); the candidate-to-index mapping assumes little-endian byte order
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the function is stateless and reentrant
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: different signature (pointer, length, NUL-terminated needle) and NOT_FOUND equals npos, but results differ from std::string::find in edge cases and it over-reads the haystack

gotchas: Correctness bugs confirmed by emulating strstr64's arithmetic in Python (the C++ was not built): the borrow in the has-zero test flags a byte equal to 0x01 directly above a real candidate, and memcmp checks only needle[1..k-1], so 'abb' in 'a`bb' returns 1 instead of not-found and 'all' in 'xx a`ll yy all' returns 4 instead of 11; the bound 'i < n - k' with step 8 skips start position n-k when n-k is a multiple of 8 (needle equal to the haystack, or 'XYZ' at offset 16 of a 19-byte string, returns not-found); n < k makes n - k wrap and the scan runs past the buffer; an empty needle indexes needle[-1].

Reads up to 5 bytes past the haystack's NUL terminator (block loads and memcmp at offsets up to n+5); the test harness gets away with it only because std::string storage sits inside a larger malloc chunk.

Harness flaw: analyze.py has no bucket for speedups between 1.0 and 2.0, so classify() returns None for them and print_summary never prints that class while still counting it in the total; the histogram that backs the '2-3x' claim hides every word where the gain was under 2x, and its percentages do not sum to 100.

Harness flaw: each word is timed as 10 calls between gettimeofday readings (1 us resolution, no warm-up, one run) on words taken from the searched text, so most searches stop near the start; a 0 us custom time prints 'faster inf' and lands in the 6x-and-up bucket, and both at 0 us prints 'same speed'. The 'custom vs strlen' heading is really custom vs libc strstr.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Never for production: pick sse4-strstr (catalogued in string-search-and-hashing) for a fixed SWAR fallback or SIMD versions, sliceslice in Rust, or Ron Charlton's strstr.c for portable C; this entry is useful only as the historical first version of the first/last-byte filter.
verified_claims_summary: The only claim is the README sentence 'faster 2-3 times than C++ std::string::find', with no stored output, CPU or compiler version, from a harness (g++ -O3, i386.txt word list, 10-call gettimeofday timing) whose histogram omits the 1-2x class. The author's later sse4-strstr results for the corrected SWAR code, on the same i386.txt word workload, show 1.70x (ARMv7, GCC 4.9.2) and 3.93x (ARMv8, clang 3.8.0) over std::string::find, but 2.1-3.0x slower than the libc strstr row on four x86 CPUs (derived from page data; libc version not stated).
status_note: Abandoned: the strstr directory's last commit is 2016-01-17 and the code was superseded by sse4-strstr in 2016; BSD-2-Clause and tiny, but it should not be vendored without the v2 fixes.
